demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 61, a woman from Oceania who has spent most of her adult life working in places where she is expected to stay calm when other people panic. For years, she has worked as a security guard in office buildings, warehouses, and shopping complexes, the kind of job where people notice her only when something has gone wrong. She likes the order of it, the routine of checking doors, logging incidents, walking the same routes until the spaces become familiar. She lives alone and has for a long time. She says she has always managed well enough on her own.

The event she returns to again and again happened on an ordinary evening shift nearly two years ago. She had been working at a loading area behind a commercial building, checking access at a gate where delivery vehicles came and went. It was near the end of the day, and there had already been tension with people trying to enter through the wrong lane. She remembers feeling tired, irritated, and determined to keep things moving safely. A man she did not know approached on foot from the side of the gate, angry that he had been told to wait. She remembers his raised voice, the sudden way he stepped into the path of a reversing forklift, and the split second in which she shouted and waved, trying to stop both of them. She moved toward the emergency barrier control and hit the wrong switch in the confusion. The barrier dropped abruptly. The forklift driver braked hard, swerved, and the pedestrian was knocked down and badly injured.

She did not see every detail clearly, but her mind has filled in the gaps so many times that now it plays like a sharp, unforgiving film. She hears the crack of impact, the man’s cry, the shouting afterward. She remembers kneeling on concrete that smelled of oil and dust, seeing blood where it should not have been, and feeling a coldness spread through her body even before the ambulance arrived. In the days that follow, she tells everyone the same facts, over and over: it was an accident, it happened fast, she was trying to help. None of those sentences settles inside her.

At first, she expects the worst feelings to pass. Instead, they harden. Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She wakes just before dawn with her heart pounding, already hearing the metallic slam of the barrier. Sometimes she dreams that she is back at the gate, except in the dream her hand keeps pressing the button again and again while the injured man looks directly at her, as if asking why. She stops watching television because sudden shouts or scenes of people falling make her whole body jerk. At work, the beep of reversing vehicles sends a flash of heat through her chest. She tells herself to breathe, to stay professional, but her hands tremble when she writes in the logbook.

She begins avoiding the loading area whenever she can. If another guard offers to cover the back gate, she agrees too quickly. She takes longer routes during patrol to avoid passing the barrier controls. When she cannot avoid those areas, she feels detached, as if she is walking through a place that belongs to someone else. She becomes watchful in a way that exhausts her. She scans for movement, listens for engines, notices every person coming too close to a vehicle. At home, that vigilance does not switch off. She checks the locks repeatedly, startles at footsteps in the corridor, and sits with the television on low volume just so the apartment does not feel too quiet.

The worst part for her is not fear but blame. She speaks about the injured man as if she has no right to complain because he is the one whose body was broken. She says she “did that” even when others remind her it was chaotic and no one intended harm. She has begun arranging her life around that belief. She no longer meets former coworkers for coffee because she is certain they see her as careless. When her sister calls from overseas, she keeps the conversation short and says she is just tired. She used to be known as steady, practical, the one who could sort things out. Now even small mistakes—misplacing her keys, missing a bus, forgetting to buy milk—bring a rush of self-contempt out of proportion to the moment.

She remains in the same line of work, though each shift feels like a test she is failing privately. She arrives early so she can compose herself before anyone sees her. She studies emergency procedures compulsively, reading incident protocols late into the night as if perfect knowledge could undo one irreversible second. She notices that she has become less patient with the public and then feels ashamed about that too. Some days she stands at an entrance in full uniform, greeting people and checking badges, while inside she is bracing against images she cannot keep out.

In session, she speaks quietly and in sequence, as if accuracy might protect her from judgment. Yet when she reaches the moment her hand hits the wrong switch, her face changes. She stares at the floor, shoulders tight, and says she can still feel the button under her thumb. She says the world is divided into before that moment and after it. Since then, she has carried herself like someone dangerous in ways other people cannot see.
